Space Apps submission — copy-paste answers

Everything here is written to be pasted into the submission form. It is honest about what is simulated; do not "improve" it by claiming real sensor data.

Project summary (174 words)

NASA Bio Monitor is a two-device prototype of a crew health monitor for a long Mars transit. A Windows application runs a deterministic simulation of six months of spaceflight — galactic cosmic radiation, cabin CO₂, microgravity, sleep and workload — and turns it into simulated physiology for a crew of five. An Android app, one phone per crew member, shows the same data and lets a crew member file a symptom report with a photo.

The important part is not the numbers but the reasoning. Every reading is compared with that crew member's own learned baseline, never a population average, and every warning explains what moved, by how much, and what to do next. Findings are grouped by health domain and hazard tier, acknowledged with a name, a time and a reason, and kept in a log.

The prototype shows how an isolated crew facing a long communication delay could triage its own health without a flight surgeon awake. All physiological data is simulated. The two apps, the database, the alert logic and the build pipeline are real and work.

Project details

What it does. The Windows application is the mission console: it holds the crew roster, runs the simulation, evaluates the health domains, raises and resolves alerts, and stores everything in SQLite. The Android app is the crew side: a crew member signs in, sees their own record, receives the same alerts, and reports symptoms, wellness, exercise and medication with an optional photo. Reports written on the phone appear in the desktop log within a second.

How it works. A Rust simulation produces a timestamped series for each signal — heart rate, heart-rate variability, respiration, temperature, SpO₂, blood pressure, sleep, activity, cabin CO₂ and radiation dose — driven by scenario events (a solar particle event, a dust storm, a workload spike, a resupply). Analysis compares each reading with a baseline learned over the first 30 simulated days, per crew member, and computes a 0-100 deviation index per health domain. Thresholds raise findings in four countermeasure tiers. Each finding carries an explanation and a recommended action, so the console is never a red light with no reason.

Why it matters. On a Mars transit the round-trip communication delay is between roughly 8 and 40 minutes. A crew cannot wait for a flight surgeon on the ground to interpret a trend, and a single clinician on board cannot watch five people continuously. Software that learns each person's normal, explains its reasoning, and keeps an auditable acknowledgement log is the difference between noise and a decision.

Tools. Rust (axum, sqlx, tokio) for the server and simulation, SQLite for storage, Tauri v2 for the Windows shell, React + TypeScript for the console, Expo / React Native for Android, GitLab CI for both builds. No cloud dependency: the desktop binary contains the entire backend.

Creativity and choices we made. We deliberately refused population reference ranges as the primary signal, because a crew member's normal is not the population's normal and microgravity shifts it further. We kept cabin hazards (CO₂, radiation) separate from personal health domains, so a crew member never sees "you are sick" when the spacecraft is the problem. We made every alert explainable and dismissible with a reason, because an alert nobody can act on trains a crew to ignore alerts. The mobile app redacts nothing but adds nothing either: one phone, one crew member, one record.

Honest limits. The physiology is simulated by our own model, not measured. The thresholds are informed by published guidance but are not clinical decisions. This is not a medical device and makes no diagnosis.
